transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-05
- Time: 16:00 PT
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Natarajan (Vertex CTO), Tom Benton (ML Eng), Eric Sun (Infra)

Summary:
Quick kickoff to understand Vertex Labs' plan to move inference from an in-house vLLM/TGI stack to Redwood. Main concerns: model compatibility (weights, tokenizers), quantization parity, latency vs cost, KV cache behavior, and security/compliance for potential private deployment. Agreed to share benchmarks and pilot options.

Topics covered (auto-generated): model compatibility, TGI quirks, quantization, eval parity, deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private), SOC2/KMS/SSO requirements, next steps.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, we are Maya and Diego from Redwood, happy to run through the portability questions. How are you all?
[00:06] Priya Natarajan: Hi Maya, doing well, thanks. We are excited but cautious, there's a lot riding on parity with our current stack.
[00:12] Diego Ramos: Totally. Maybe to start, can you give us a high-level of what you run today? Models, infra, typical p50/p95 latencies, that sort of thing.
[00:20] Tom Benton: Sure, quick overview — we run a mix of Llama-derived models and some custom finetunes with vLLM on top of Text-Generation-Infrastructure (TGI). Production runs on k8s with GPU pools, tokenization is BPE-ish, we do int8 quantization with bitsandbytes for cost. P50 is usually ~180ms per request for short prompts, p95 jumps to ~700ms with long context and heavy KV reuse.
[00:40] Eric Sun: For infra, we have strict egress rules, everything inside our VPC but most of the serving stack is managed by internal infra.
[00:47] Maya Chen: That's helpful. Two main migration paths: 1) Hosted Redwood API to get started fast, 2) Dedicated pools to preserve throughput predictability, and 3) Private deployment behind your VPC for compliance. Which of those are you leaning to?
[01:03] Priya Natarajan: Ideally private but we want to prototyping on hosted or dedicated first. We need to validate eval parity before we commit to private.
[01:12] Diego Ramos: Makes sense. On compatibility — are your models normal HF-compatible checkpoints or are there TGI-specific wrappers/patches?
[01:20] Tom Benton: Mostly HF checkpoints but we've applied a few hooks for streaming and some custom sampling we built into TGI. Also tokenizer variants - we have small tokenization differences that affect exact logprobs.
[01:32] Diego Ramos: Ok so two areas to watch: tokenizer alignment and runtime sampling hooks. For tokenizer we can run a seed set of inputs to compare tokenization outputs; for sampling hooks we can mirror your sampling parameters in Redwood but if you've got C-level custom code we'd need the code paths.
[01:47] Priya Natarajan: Right — we can provide tokenization seeds and our sampling config. How does Redwood handle quantized models? Bitsandbytes int8 isn't always identical across runtimes.
[01:58] Maya Chen: Our runtime supports quantized execution and we have recommended quantization profiles. There are sometimes small numeric differences with int8 across kernels. We surface quality regression alerts in Redwood Optimize and suggest fallback to fp16 for critical workloads.
[02:12] Tom Benton: What's the effort to re-run our evals? We have a fixed eval set with rouge/bleu variants plus human ratings for hallucination.
[02:20] Diego Ramos: We typically ask customers to share the eval dataset and scripts. We'll run an automated parity suite comparing logits, generated outputs, and our fidelity metrics. We also recommend a small A/B with traffic splitting — canary on Dedicated or Hosted with traffic routing.
[02:33] Eric Sun: Network question — for private deployment, will Redwood require outgoing connections to the control plane? We need to know about egress and if HSM/KMS calls travel outside.
[02:42] Maya Chen: Short answer yes, the control plane for Private requires a management channel to Redwood endpoints unless you choose the fully air-gapped on-prem package. For KMS, we support bringing-your-own KMS or HSM integrations; keys do not leave your tenancy. We can share our security whitepaper — SOC2, SSO (SAML/OKTA), and audit logs.
[03:00] Priya Natarajan: Good, we'll want the whitepaper and the audit log format.
[03:04] Tom Benton: Back to performance — vLLM has specific KV cache behaviors that let reuse cut p95 dramatically. How does Redwood's KV cache work for long-context reuse?
[03:13] Diego Ramos: We do continuous KV caching and prefix caching. For workloads with heavy reuse we can pin warm KV caches and use sticky routing to keep requests on the same GPU pool. Also batching policies can be tuned to match your tail latency SLO.
[03:26] Tom Benton: Any limitations on sequence length? We're pushing 32k in some internal experiments.
[03:31] Diego Ramos: We support long context but the runtime-cost grows. For 32k we'd look at memory-optimized instances and quantization strategies. We'll need to run benchmarks to estimate TCO and latency.
[03:40] Priya Natarajan: On the dev side, how invasive is the API change? Our product is built against TGI endpoints.
[03:46] Maya Chen: Our API is REST/SDK first with structured outputs and function call support. For minimal code changes you can front our API with a shim — we also offer client SDKs in Python/TS. Diego can walk through a mapping doc of common TGI calls to Redwood equivalents.
[03:58] Diego Ramos: I can prepare a mapping table (TGI endpoint -> Redwood call pattern, headers, sampling params). Also will include examples for streaming and function-call style responses.
[04:08] Tom Benton: Great. Another concern: cost. Our current cost model is GPU hours + storage; we need an apples-to-apples cost comparison.
[04:16] Maya Chen: We'll provide unit economics — tokens/sec, infra cost with and without quant, and a recommended Dedicated config to match throughput. Redwood Optimize will also recommend batching and cache settings to reduce unit cost.
[04:27] Priya Natarajan: Can Redwood replicate our finetune pipeline or do we have to re-export models? We have a couple finetuned checkpoints with custom metadata.
[04:35] Diego Ramos: We generally accept HF-style checkpoints and custom metadata as blobs. If you have non-standard format we can work with you on a conversion script; we do a model onboarding pass that tests load, tokenization, and sample inference.
[04:45] Eric Sun: About data retention — how long do you keep inputs/outputs for hosted vs dedicated vs private? We need strict retention controls for PSD and customer PII.
[04:54] Maya Chen: Hosted stores logs per our retention policy; for Dedicated you can set retention and log forwarding; for Private you control retention entirely. We can support no-logs options and redaction plugins.
[05:05] Tom Benton: Any known parity issues porting from TGI/vLLM? Anything we should expect to break?
[05:12] Diego Ramos: The common quirks are tokenizer mismatch, minor sampling RNG differences, and kernel-level quantization noise. Business logic tied to exact logits may need an A/B. Also streaming semantics sometimes differ; TGI has a particular chunking pattern. We'll capture those in the parity report.
[05:28] Priya Natarajan: Sounds reasonable. What's the timeline you recommend for a pilot?
[05:32] Maya Chen: Pilot in 3 phases: 1) Onboard models + tokenization check (1 week), 2) Perf benchmarks and parity runs (1-2 weeks), 3) Canary traffic and rollback policies (1 week). So roughly 3–4 weeks end-to-end for a solid pilot.
[05:47] Tom Benton: That fits our internal Q2 goals. We'll need an internal exec summary for procurement.
[05:52] Maya Chen: We'll send a one-page exec summary + pricing bands for Hosted / Dedicated / Private.
[05:57] Eric Sun: For private, what's the support model and SLA?
[06:00] Maya Chen: Private gets enterprise SLAs and support tiers; Dedicated has an SLA too. We'll include SLA terms and response times in the pricing doc.
[06:07] Priya Natarajan: OK, can you also include a sample run for tokenization diffs so our team can see differences quickly?
[06:12] Diego Ramos: Yes, Diego will send a tokenization comparator tool and a small script that runs your seeds and returns diff stats.
[06:18] Tom Benton: Perfect. Any blockers from our side for the first step?
[06:21] Maya Chen: We need your eval set, a couple of model checkpoints (or pointers), and network constraints for private. That'll let Diego kick off the onboarding.
[06:30] Priya Natarajan: We'll assemble that and aim to get it to you by 2026-03-10.
[06:33] Maya Chen: Great. Quick recap of next steps...
[06:35] Maya Chen: I'll send pricing and pilot options by 2026-03-07; Diego will share benchmark template and tokenization comparator by 2026-03-09; Vertex will provide workloads by 2026-03-10; schedule perf run week of 2026-03-16. Any questions?
[06:48] Tom Benton: No, that's clear. Thanks everyone.
[06:51] Priya Natarajan: Thank you, talk soon.
[06:53] Maya Chen: Thanks all, bye.
